title: Nilometers of Egypt
summary: Nilometers were wells, staircases or rock-cut gauges used to measure the Nile's annual flood, which signalled the harvest and helped set taxes. EBSCO credits Sesostris I, who ruled 1971-1926 BCE, with the first, and National Geographic dates one at Thmuis to the third century BCE; fewer than two dozen are known.

uncertainty.note: EBSCO attributes the first nilometer to Sesostris I, written as ruling 1971-26 B.C.E. (astronomical -1970 to -1926). National Geographic says a nilometer found at Thmuis was likely built in the third century B.C. and used for roughly a thousand years, so use continued long after the range given. The attribution to one king is the source's wording and was not independently confirmed.

as_recorded.value: Likely constructed during the third century B.C.

when.display: attributed to Sesostris I (ruled 1971-1926 BCE); in use for centuries after

where.modern_name: Elephantine Island, Aswan, Egypt (one of the oldest known sites; nilometers lie along the Nile)
where.historical_name: Elephantine, on the Nile in ancient Egypt

importance.justification: Flood gauges let rulers forecast harvests and fix tax levies in a country that depended on the Nile.

sources.title: History of energy in Ancient Egypt
Ancient Device for Determining Taxes Discovered in Egypt
sources.author: Nick Romeo

reviewer_note: Least sure of the date: the id suggests c. 600 BCE, but the opened sources give a Middle Kingdom attribution (EBSCO, unverified) and a third-century BCE example; I dated from their wording. The pin at Elephantine follows EBSCO's list of oldest finds; the place of the earliest nilometer is uncertain.
